The Dual Government (1765–72) After the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) Clive took the Diwani (revenue and civil justice) but left the Nizamat (police, criminal justice, defence) to the Nawab, who was paid a fixed sum (Rs 53 lakh). Why? The Company lacked trained staff, feared European rivals and Parliament, and could use Indian deputies to avoid blame. Indian deputies did the work: Muhammad Reza Khan (Naib Diwan of Bengal, also deputy Nazim) and Raja Shitab Roy (Naib Diwan of Bihar). Effect: the Company had power without responsibility; the Nawab had responsibility without power. Revenue was squeezed, peasants and artisans suffered, and the 1770 famine killed about a third of Bengal's people. Ended in 1772 by Warren Hastings; Reza Khan and Shitab Roy were removed and tried. Sir John Macpherson (1785–86, acting) and Lord Cornwallis (1786–1793) Cornwallis gave British India its permanent machinery: the Permanent Settlement, the Cornwallis Code, a police system and a professional civil service. Charter Act, 1833 GG of Bengal became GG of India, with full civil, military and legislative powers over all British India; Madras and Bombay lost their legislative powers. The same Metcalfe, aged 23, had negotiated the Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with Ranjit Singh. Civil services Cornwallis (1786–93) is the Father of the Civil Service in India: he turned the Company's corrupt trading clerks into a paid, rule-bound administrative service, but kept Indians out of its higher posts. Everything after him is a slow fight over two questions: how to recruit (patronage or exam) and whether Indians get in. Stage 1: Company servants become administrators (1765–1806) Before Cornwallis, Company servants were paid little and earned through private trade, gifts and bribes. Clive and Hastings tried to stop this, with little success. Cornwallis's reforms: high salaries; private trade and gifts banned; promotion by seniority, so officers were not dependent on favour.
